And the tightening test found a second defect immediately.

A ceiling on citation chains is about HEIGHT, not recursion depth.

Any independently implemented producer emitting another key order would have hit exactly this

8. One instrument finding, and three questions
The grid probe threw on a shorthand slip and failed closed.
all six behavioural booleans read false at once
. Right direction, still a gate you must read twice — six simultaneous falses are a bug in the instrument, one false is a defect. Worth a rule: a behavioural block should probably report
it returned false, not only that it did.
Q1 — the independent producer, and what it should be allowed to import.
Your constraint is that it must not import the JS canonicalizer, bundle builders or schemas, and must implement from frozen protocol text.
The protocol text does not exist yet.

The grammar, scope, child table, reference contract, chain derivation and policy are all declared inside checkers as executable data, and the spec states none of them. So the first half of that round is writing the wire specification — which is also the only real test of whether P4.1's five planes are describable rather than merely implemented. Do you want that as a document in this tree, or as the producer's own README derived by reading the checkers, so that a disagreement between spec and code shows up as a disagreement between two humans rather than one?
Q2 — which language, and does it get its own JCS?
A second JS implementation shares Node's
and its duplicate-key resolution, which is exactly the hazard I closed by construction rather than by test. A producer in a language whose parser keeps the FIRST duplicate would make that hazard
instead of theoretical. That argues for Python or Go over TypeScript, and against reusing any JCS library that was validated against the same vectors I used.
Q3 — should the independent producer be given a REFUSING artifact to reproduce, not only a passing one?
Every cross-implementation test I can think of checks that two implementations agree about a VERIFIED artifact. The sharper test is whether they agree about
a forged artifact draws — that is where a protocol's semantics actually live, and where two implementations that agree on the happy path routinely diverge.
